::: {.callout-note}
## Original course-project chapter

This chapter is the course-project team's original analysis, written by
teammates and kept as submitted. The only changes are shared data fixes
and small cleanups (computed instead of hardcoded dates, clearer names);
the methods were not revised for this portfolio. Known limitations:

- **Possibly spurious levels regression.** The target, inflation and
  unemployment behave like trending series (see the unit-root tests below),
  and regressing trending series on each other can show strong
  relationships that are not real. A partial-adjustment model (the lagged
  target as a regressor, used below only as a robustness check) is the
  standard way to estimate a policy rule.
- **Standard errors ignore autocorrelation.** Monthly errors are strongly
  correlated over time, so the ordinary p-values overstate how certain each
  estimate is. Newey-West (autocorrelation-robust) errors would be wider.
- **Zero-lower-bound months are included.** In 2009–2015 and 2020–2022 the
  target could not fall below zero, so it stayed flat whatever the economy
  did. Those months pull every estimated response toward zero.
- **Lasso screening.** It is given `core_pce_yoy` and `inflation_gap`
  (the same series shifted by 2), uses random cross-validation folds on
  time-series data, and its result is not used afterwards.
- **Break tests reject everywhere.** The Chow tests assume independent
  errors and reject stability at every date tested, and BIC selects the
  maximum number of breaks allowed, so neither pins down when the rule
  changed. The number of breaks is therefore a fixed setting.
:::


This section studies how the federal funds target is related to selected macroeconomic and financial variables, and whether those relationships remain stable over time.

## Variable Selection

```{r}
data_rq1 <- df_final %>%
  arrange(date)

vars <- c(
  "ff_target",
  "core_pce_yoy", "inflation_gap",
  "UNRATE", "payems_yoy",
  "term_spread_10y_3m", "BAA10Y", "ANFCI",
  "fomc_meetings", "days_since_last_fomc"
)

df_full_rq1 <- data_rq1[, vars]
na_ratio <- colMeans(is.na(df_full_rq1))
df_clean_rq1 <- df_full_rq1[, na_ratio < 0.2]
```

```{r}
x <- model.matrix(ff_target ~ ., df_clean_rq1)[, -1]
y <- df_clean_rq1$ff_target

lasso <- cv.glmnet(x, y, alpha = 1)

coef(lasso, s = "lambda.min")
```

Variable selection narrows the model to a smaller set of predictors that appear most relevant to the policy rate.

## Final Regression Dataset

```{r}
df_reg_rq1 <- data_rq1[, c(
  "date", "ff_target", "core_pce_yoy", "UNRATE",
  "term_spread_10y_3m", "BAA10Y", "ANFCI"
)]
```

The regression section uses a focused set of explanatory variables rather than the full macro dataset.

## Exploratory Time-Series Checks

```{r}
plot(df_reg_rq1$date, df_reg_rq1$ff_target, type = "l", main = "Federal Funds Target Rate")

plot(df_reg_rq1$date, df_reg_rq1$core_pce_yoy, type = "l", main = "Core PCE Inflation (YoY %)")

plot(df_reg_rq1$date, df_reg_rq1$UNRATE, type = "l", main = "Unemployment Rate")

plot(df_reg_rq1$date, df_reg_rq1$term_spread_10y_3m, type = "l", main = "Term Spread")

cor(df_reg_rq1[, -1], use = "complete.obs")
```

These plots and the correlation matrix give a first look at the time-series behavior and cross-variable relationships before formal estimation.

## ADF Tests

```{r}
adf.test(df_reg_rq1$ff_target)
adf.test(df_reg_rq1$core_pce_yoy)
adf.test(df_reg_rq1$UNRATE)
adf.test(df_reg_rq1$term_spread_10y_3m)
adf.test(df_reg_rq1$BAA10Y)
adf.test(df_reg_rq1$ANFCI)
```

The ADF tests motivate the later robustness checks in differences and the stability analysis.

## Baseline Model

```{r}
model_baseline <- lm(
  ff_target ~ core_pce_yoy + UNRATE + term_spread_10y_3m + BAA10Y + ANFCI,
  data = df_reg_rq1
)

summary(model_baseline)
```

The baseline model estimates the full-sample association between the policy rate and the selected explanatory variables.

## Robustness Check 1: Dynamic Model

```{r}
df_reg_rq1$ff_target_lag1 <- dplyr::lag(df_reg_rq1$ff_target, 1)

model_dyn <- lm(
  ff_target ~ ff_target_lag1 + core_pce_yoy + UNRATE +
    term_spread_10y_3m + BAA10Y + ANFCI,
  data = df_reg_rq1
)

summary(model_dyn)
```

The dynamic specification captures persistence in the policy rate through a lagged dependent variable.

## Robustness Check 2: Differenced Model

```{r}
df_diff <- data.frame(
  date = df_reg_rq1$date[-1],
  d_ff = diff(df_reg_rq1$ff_target),
  d_core_pce = diff(df_reg_rq1$core_pce_yoy),
  d_unrate = diff(df_reg_rq1$UNRATE),
  term_spread_10y_3m = df_reg_rq1$term_spread_10y_3m[-1]
)

model_diff <- lm(
  d_ff ~ d_core_pce + d_unrate + term_spread_10y_3m,
  data = df_diff
)

summary(model_diff)
```

The first-difference model checks whether the main relationships remain visible when the focus shifts from levels to short-run changes.

## Rolling Coefficient Plots

```{r}
get_coef <- function(idx) {
  window_data <- df_reg_rq1[idx, ]
  coef(lm(
    ff_target ~ core_pce_yoy + UNRATE +
      term_spread_10y_3m + BAA10Y + ANFCI,
    data = window_data
  ))
}

roll <- rollapply(
  data = 1:nrow(df_reg_rq1),
  width = 60,
  FUN = get_coef,
  by = 1,
  align = "right"
)

roll <- as.data.frame(roll)
roll_dates <- df_reg_rq1$date[60:nrow(df_reg_rq1)]
```

```{r}
plot(roll_dates, roll$core_pce_yoy, type = "l",
     main = "Rolling Coefficient: core_pce_yoy",
     xlab = "Date", ylab = "Coefficient")

plot(roll_dates, roll$UNRATE, type = "l",
     main = "Rolling Coefficient: UNRATE",
     xlab = "Date", ylab = "Coefficient")

plot(roll_dates, roll$term_spread_10y_3m, type = "l",
     main = "Rolling Coefficient: Term Spread",
     xlab = "Date", ylab = "Coefficient")
```

Rolling coefficients provide a visual way to assess whether the reaction function changes across different periods.

## Breakpoint Analysis

```{r}
rq1_formula <- ff_target ~ core_pce_yoy + UNRATE +
  term_spread_10y_3m + BAA10Y + ANFCI

bp <- breakpoints(rq1_formula, data = df_reg_rq1, breaks = BP_MAX_BREAKS)

summary(bp)
plot(bp)
```

```{r}
# Number of breaks is a setting (BP_N_BREAKS); the dates come from the fitted
# model. BIC's own choice is printed for comparison.
bic_breaks <- length(breakpoints(bp)$breakpoints)
bic_breaks

bp_rows  <- breakpoints(bp, breaks = BP_N_BREAKS)$breakpoints
n_breaks <- length(bp_rows)
bp_dates <- df_reg_rq1$date[bp_rows]

n_breaks
bp_dates
confint(bp, breaks = n_breaks)
```

```{r}
plot(df_reg_rq1$date, df_reg_rq1$ff_target, type = "l")
abline(v = bp_dates, col = "red")
```

The analysis uses `r n_breaks` breaks, estimated at `r paste(format(bp_dates, "%b %Y"), collapse = ", ")`. BIC alone would pick `r bic_breaks`, the most the test allows; with trending variables and serially correlated errors BIC tends to over-select breaks, so the number of breaks is kept as an explicit choice.

## Chow Tests

```{r}
chow_dates <- sort(unique(c(CHOW_EVENT_DATES, bp_dates)))

for (d in as.list(chow_dates)) {
  idx <- which(df_reg_rq1$date == d)
  if (length(idx) > 0) {
    test <- sctest(rq1_formula, type = "Chow", point = idx, data = df_reg_rq1)
    cat("Date:", format(d),
        if (d %in% bp_dates) "(estimated break)" else "(event)",
        "| F =", round(test$statistic, 2),
        "| p-value =", format(test$p.value, scientific = TRUE), "\n")
  }
}
```

The Chow tests evaluate whether the regression relationship shifts at both estimated and theory-motivated break dates.

## Sub-Period Regressions

```{r}
# Sub-periods run between the estimated break dates.
period_starts <- c(min(df_reg_rq1$date), bp_dates)
period_ends   <- c(bp_dates, max(df_reg_rq1$date) + 1)
period_labels <- paste0(format(period_starts, "%Y"), "-", format(period_ends - 1, "%Y"))

df_reg_rq1$period <- cut(
  df_reg_rq1$date,
  breaks = c(period_starts, max(df_reg_rq1$date) + 1),
  labels = period_labels,
  right = FALSE
)

models <- lapply(period_labels, function(p) {
  lm(rq1_formula, data = subset(df_reg_rq1, period == p))
})
names(models) <- period_labels

lapply(models, summary)
```

```{r}
coef_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(models, coef))
coef_table
```

```{r}
coef_table <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(models), function(p) {
  df <- tidy(models[[p]])
  df$period <- p
  return(df)
}))

coef_table
```

```{r}
ggplot(coef_table[coef_table$term != "(Intercept)", ],
       aes(x = period, y = estimate, color = term, group = term)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point()
```

Sub-period regressions make it easier to interpret how the policy rule differs across historical regimes.
